common_name: L.D. Braithwaite Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; L.D. Braithwaite is valued for its rich crimson color and can be kept compact with regular pruning or allowed to grow taller against a low support.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune back by about a third in late winter to keep the framework productive and shapely. Introduced by David Austin in 1988 and named for a nurseryman friend of the breeder, L.D. Braithwaite bears loosely cupped, velvety crimson-red blooms that hold their rich color well even in hot weather, though the fragrance is lighter than in many other English roses. Its vigorous, upright growth can be kept as a bushy border shrub with regular pruning or allowed to grow taller against a low support, and it repeat-flowers dependably from late spring through frost. Watch for blackspot in humid climates and provide good air circulation to keep foliage cleaner through summer.
sources: David Austin Roses — L.D. Braithwaite variety notes

common_name: Molineux Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun; Molineux stays more compact than many English roses, making it well suited to smaller borders or large containers.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and deadhead through the season to keep new flushes coming on this compact shrub. Introduced by David Austin in 1994 and named for the Wolverhampton football stadium near the breeder's nursery, Molineux bears richly saturated, deep egg-yolk-yellow rosette blooms with a sweet fragrance carrying a hint of violet, held on a tidy, well-branched bush that stays smaller than many English roses. Its compact habit and strong repeat bloom from late spring through frost make it a good choice for a smaller border or large container where a full-sized shrub rose would crowd its neighbors. Prune canes back by about a third in late winter to maintain a dense, floriferous shape.

common_name: Pat Austin Rose (Copper-Orange David Austin English Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation and a support if trained as a climber; Pat Austin is known for its unusual copper-orange color and can be grown as a large shrub or short climber.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a support if training the vigorous canes as a short climber. Introduced by David Austin in 2004 and named for the breeder's wife, Pat Austin bears striking, loosely double blooms in a warm burnt-orange to copper on the face with a paler coppery-yellow reverse, an unusual color combination among English roses, carried on vigorous, arching canes with a lighter tea fragrance than most Austin varieties. It can be kept pruned as a large rounded shrub or trained upward on a fence or pillar for extra height, and it repeat-blooms in flushes from late spring through fall. Deadhead regularly and provide good air circulation, since its vigorous growth benefits from occasional thinning to keep the center of the plant open.

common_name: Dame Judi Dench Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Dame Judi Dench bears unusually large blooms and benefits from routine feeding and deadheading to sustain repeat flowering.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2017 and named for the celebrated actress, Dame Judi Dench bears very large, informally cupped blooms in warm apricot-orange tones with a strong, fruity tea fragrance, opening on a robust, well-branched shrub bred for improved disease resistance. It flowers generously from late spring through frost and its large flower size and bold color make it a strong focal point in a mixed border. Deadhead spent blooms through the season to sustain repeat flowering.

common_name: Gabriel Oak Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Gabriel Oak is a vigorous, disease-resistant shrub that pairs thematically with the earlier Austin rose Bathsheba, both named for characters in the same Thomas Hardy novel.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2019 and named for the steadfast shepherd of Thomas Hardy's Far from the Madding Crowd — the same novel that gave the earlier Austin rose Bathsheba its name — Gabriel Oak bears large, rounded, rich rose-pink blooms with a strong, fruity fragrance, held on a vigorous, healthy shrub bred with good disease resistance. It repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost, and its sizable flowers and robust constitution suit both a mixed border and a dedicated rose bed. Deadhead through the season to keep successive flushes coming.

Deadhead spent blooms regularly to sustain the flowering cycle.
